opportunities.gap: The equity backbone of the section (the recurring 'nine students with no reliable home device,' 'reliable home laptops encodes a class assumption') is the strongest claim yet is supported only by a reused unnamed datafication DOI and a generic 'critical edtech studies' link. Selwyn is never named and there is no home-access/digital-divide statistic. NOTE FROM RESEARCH: the datafication DOI 10.1080/17439884.2020.1686017 already IS a Selwyn work (Perrotta & Selwyn 2019), so Selwyn is cited but invisible; naming him also resolves part of the currency item.
opportunities.proposed_change: Add a one-line 'Recent Evidence' callout near the Core Concept 'Critical edtech studies' bullet (line 33) that names Selwyn explicitly and anchors the home-access claim to a current digital-divide statistic. Concrete wording: 'Recent evidence: NCES (2021) reports 6% of children in the lowest income quartile lacked home internet versus 1% in the highest; the scenario's nine-of-28 figure is an instance of this documented homework gap, not just a narrative number (see Selwyn on critical edtech).' Reframe '9 of 28 with no reliable home device' as an instance of a documented access disparity.

sources.cite: NCES, Condition of Education — Children's Internet Access at Home (2021 data)
sources.finding: In 2021, 3% of children ages 3-18 had no home internet access overall; by income quartile, ~6% in the lowest quartile lacked access versus ~1% in the highest, and cost was the main barrier for families earning under $40,000. This grounds the 'no reliable home device' equity claim in a real, current access disparity.

opportunities.gap: The two load-bearing empirical claims of the section carry no citation: 'facial-recognition error rates are documented to be higher for darker-skinned students' (Self-Explain line 77; Textbook Walkthrough line 97) and 'a model trained mostly on standard-English essays flags non-standard phrasing as errors' (Core Concept line 28; Worked Example line 48). In a course whose thesis is evidence-grounded judgment, presenting documented fairness findings as uncited assertions is the weakest spot.
opportunities.proposed_change: Add a one-to-two sentence 'Recent Evidence' callout after Core Concept (after line 36), or inline citations at first mention. (1) Facial-recognition disparity: anchor to Buolamwini & Gebru 'Gender Shades' (2018) and the NIST FRVT Part 3: Demographic Effects report (NISTIR 8280, 2019), noting NIST found demographic differentials in the majority of algorithms tested, with elevated false positives for African American and Asian faces in one-to-many matching. (2) Standard-English/ELL essay-scoring bias: anchor to Wilson & Huang (2024) in Assessing Writing, which found evidence of bias in automated essay scores for English language learners. Link by DOI where one exists; Gender Shades has no DOI (PMLR proceedings) so link the proceedings PDF.
opportunities.where_to_apply: 04.mdx — add 'Recent Evidence' note after Core Concept (after line 36); or inline at Worked Example line 48 (AES claim) and Textbook Walkthrough line 97 (facial-recognition claim). Add matching entries to References (lines 153-158).

sources.cite: Buolamwini & Gebru (2018) Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification
sources.finding: Commercial gender-classification systems had far higher error rates for darker-skinned subjects (up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women) vs lighter-skinned men (0.8%), establishing skin-tone disparity in face analysis. No DOI (PMLR v81 proceedings).

sources.cite: Grother, Ngan & Hanaoka / NIST (2019) FRVT Part 3: Demographic Effects (NISTIR 8280)
sources.finding: NIST found empirical evidence of demographic differentials in the majority of face-recognition algorithms studied, with the highest false-positive rates in one-to-many matching for African American females; updated by FRVT Part 8 / NISTIR 8429 (pages.nist.gov/frvt). Grounds the 'documented higher error rates for darker-skinned students' claim.

sources.cite: Wilson & Huang (2024) Validity of automated essay scores for elementary-age English language learners: Evidence of bias?
sources.finding: Peer-reviewed study (Assessing Writing, v60) finding evidence of bias in automated essay scoring for ELLs, grounding the claim that models trained on standard-English writing disadvantage multilingual/non-standard phrasing.

opportunities.gap: The section repeatedly invokes 'this placement's district data policy' and the facial-recognition attendance case turns on biometric data collection from minors, yet the MDX cites NO privacy statute. FERPA and COPPA are the legal floor a field-placement equity audit of a biometric attendance system must reference.
opportunities.proposed_change: Add a brief 'Legal floor' callout in the Textbook Walkthrough facial-recognition case (lines 93-97): a sentence noting that biometric/attendance data on minors implicates FERPA (education records) and, for under-13 students, COPPA. Note the currency fact that the FTC's amended COPPA rule (finalized Jan 16, 2025; effective June 23, 2025; full compliance April 22, 2026) now explicitly classifies biometric identifiers including facial templates as covered personal information requiring verifiable parental consent. Frame the audit's monitoring check as also confirming legal-basis/consent, not only error-rate disparity.
opportunities.where_to_apply: 04.mdx — Textbook Walkthrough (lines 93-97), or a new short 'Legal floor' callout after Core Concept.

sources.cite: FTC (2025) Amended COPPA Rule — biometric identifiers
sources.finding: FTC finalized COPPA amendments Jan 16, 2025 (effective June 23, 2025; full compliance April 22, 2026) that now explicitly cover biometric identifiers capable of automated recognition, including facial templates, voiceprints, and fingerprints — directly applicable to facial-recognition attendance for under-13 students.

sources.cite: Loeb & Loeb (2025) Children's Online Privacy in 2025: The Amended COPPA Rule
sources.finding: Confirms the 2025 amended COPPA rule expands the personal-information definition to biometric data and tightens parental-consent requirements; both FERPA and COPPA can apply simultaneously to an edtech product used in schools that collects data from children under 13.

opportunities.gap: The entire section turns on the diagnosis that non-completion of at-home video was an ACCESS barrier (unreliable home time/connectivity), not unwillingness. This is precisely the documented 'homework gap' / digital-divide phenomenon, but the section never names it or cites any evidence. For a course that explicitly values evidence-grounding and critical edtech (Selwyn: 'couldn't do it' vs 'didn't do it'), the central empirical claim is uncited.
opportunities.proposed_change: Add a short 'Recent Evidence' callout (or inline citation) at the 'Critical edtech studies' bullet, line 32, naming the homework gap / home-access divide and citing current figures: roughly 15% of U.S. households with school-age children lack a high-speed home connection; about 12% of teens report being unable to complete homework due to lack of reliable computer/internet access, and 22% sometimes do homework on a cellphone; the gap is sharply income-stratified (about 44% of households under $30k income lack high-speed home internet vs about 6% of households over $75k). Frame it as: non-completion is frequently 'couldn't do it' (access), not 'didn't do it' (effort), which is exactly the context-mismatch the section teaches. Cite NCES Condition of Education (Children's Internet Access at Home) and Pew Research Center homework-gap data.
